Hi Julia — quick technical note ahead of the meeting to answer your 1–3 at a high level. Happy to go deeper in the call.

1) Noisy-neighbor mitigation (Dedicated):
- Dedicated capacity runs on reserved GPU pools mapped to a single customer namespace; we do full allocation at the host level (CUDA-visible GPUs pinned). That gives physical isolation (no other tenants on those GPUs).
- We also enforce process-level cgroups and GPU bus isolation to prevent cross-tenant interference. NUMA affinity and tuned kernel parameters reduce jitter for short requests.
- Preemption policies: on Dedicated, we avoid preemptible instances for production pools; burst/overflow can be routed to separate preemptible pools if needed (with explicit policy control).

2) Latency SLOs & fallback behavior:
- We can commit to latency SLOs at the model/route level for Dedicated capacity; specifics (e.g., 99.9th percentile) require capacity sizing and an agreed traffic profile.
- Fallbacks: Redwood supports automatic fallback to a compatible model variant (smaller quantized model) or cross-region routing when capacity saturated. We surface fallbacks as part of the route policy and log them for observability.

3) HIPAA & networking:
- Private VPC and on-prem deployments provide the strongest controls: customer-managed VPC peering, dedicated subnets, and KMS/HSM integrations for key custody. For Hosted + Dedicated we offer BA agreements and can bring in dedicated networking (VPC peering + private link) depending on contract.

Notes: caching (prefix/KV), batching strategies, and token limits will materially affect p95. For 100 qps / 350 tokens, we should size a Dedicated pool and run a short perf validation to prove p95.

Reference (internal): see infra SLA & routing policy notes: https://internal.redwood.com/infra/sla-policies (I can export a client-facing summary in the call).

If Wed/Thu afternoon PST works, I can present a sizing sketch and sample configs.
